title: Python Programming with PyCharm
subtitle: Write, run, debug and test real Python programs in a professional IDE, from your first script to a tested, version-controlled project.
outcomes: Set up Python projects in PyCharm, each with its own virtual environment and packages
Write Python programs with variables, decisions, loops, functions, collections and files
Find and fix bugs with PyCharm's debugger: breakpoints, stepping and evaluating expressions
Test your code with pytest in PyCharm's test runner, and refactor it safely
Keep your work in Git from inside the IDE
prerequisites: None: this course starts from zero. You need a Windows, macOS or Linux computer that can run PyCharm, with Python 3 installed (python.org has installers).
description: Learn Python the way professional developers work: in an IDE that understands your code. In every lesson your instructor teaches a Python idea and then shows it in PyCharm, step by step, with the keyboard shortcuts for macOS, Windows and Linux, so you learn the language and the tool together. You'll set up projects and virtual environments, write programs that make decisions, loop, and read and write files, then learn the habits that make code dependable: debugging with breakpoints instead of guesswork, testing with pytest, refactoring with the IDE's help, and keeping your history in Git. Every module ends with a hands-on lab you do in PyCharm and submit for your instructor's feedback, and the course ends with a project you build from scratch.

modules.title: Get set up: Python and PyCharm
modules.summary: Install the tools, find your way around PyCharm, and run your first program in a project with its own virtual environment.

lessons.title: What Python is, and why developers use an IDE
objectives: Describe what Python is and what it's used for
Explain what an IDE adds to a plain text editor
key_points: Python is a general-purpose programming language known for readable code; it's used for web services, data analysis, automation, scripting and AI.
Python code is run by an interpreter, a program that reads your code and carries it out; the standard interpreter is called CPython.
An IDE (integrated development environment) brings an editor, a way to run code, a debugger, testing and version control together in one place.
PyCharm is JetBrains' IDE for Python. Because it understands your code, it can complete it, point out problems as you type and change it safely across a project.
Search Everywhere, opened by pressing Shift twice, finds files, classes, symbols, actions and settings from one box.

steps.do: Open PyCharm. The Welcome screen offers New Project, Open (for a folder you already have) and Clone Repository (called Get from VCS in older versions).
Open the built-in IDE tutorials from the Help menu: Help | Learn IDE Features. They're short interactive lessons inside the IDE itself.
steps.see: A Learn panel with lessons on editing, navigation and refactoring.

steps.do: Open Search Everywhere and type 'theme' to find the setting that switches between light and dark.
Open Find Action, which finds any command by name, and type 'Reformat Code'.
steps.see: The action, with its own shortcut beside it: Find Action is how you learn shortcuts.

steps.do: Open Settings to see where everything can be changed: editor, keymap, plugins and your Python interpreters.

lessons.title: Projects, interpreters and virtual environments
objectives: Explain why each project gets its own virtual environment
Create a project with a virtual environment and install a package into it
key_points: A virtual environment is a folder with its own Python interpreter and installed packages, so the packages one project needs don't clash with another's.
PyCharm can create a virtual environment for each new project and then uses it to run your code, install packages and understand your imports.
Packages, such as requests for working with the web, are installed with pip (pip install requests) or from PyCharm's Python Packages tool window.
A requirements.txt file lists the packages a project needs, so anyone can recreate its environment with pip install -r requirements.txt.

walkthrough.title: Create a project with its own virtual environment

steps.do: On the Welcome screen click New Project and choose a plain Python project (Pure Python). Name it hello-pycharm.
Under the interpreter settings, keep the option that creates a new virtual environment (venv) inside the project, using the Python 3 you installed. Click Create.
steps.see: The project opens, and the interpreter shown in the status bar, at the bottom right, names the new environment.

steps.do: Open the Terminal tool window and check which Python it uses.
steps.see: Python 3.x, and the prompt starts with (.venv): PyCharm's terminal activates the project's environment for you.

steps.do: Open the Python Packages tool window (View | Tool Windows | Python Packages), search for requests and click Install.
steps.see: requests appears in the list of installed packages.

steps.do: Open Settings and go to Project: hello-pycharm | Python Interpreter to see every package in the environment, and the button for adding or switching interpreters.

lessons.title: Write and run your first program
objectives: Write a Python script that takes input and prints output
Run, rerun and configure scripts in PyCharm
key_points: print() shows text in the output, and input() asks the user for text, which it always returns as a string.
A variable is a name for a value; you create one by assigning to it, as in name = input('Your name? ').
PyCharm runs your script with the project's interpreter and shows what it prints in the Run tool window.
A run configuration remembers how to run a script: which file, its arguments, its working folder and its interpreter. PyCharm makes one the first time you run a file.

walkthrough.title: Create, run and rerun a script

steps.do: In the Project tool window, select the project folder and create a new Python file named greet.py.
Type the program. As you type pri, PyCharm offers print: press Enter or Tab to accept it.
steps.code:
name = input("What's your name? ")
print(f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to Python.")

steps.do: Run the file you're in: right-click in the editor and choose Run 'greet', click the green arrow in the gutter, or use the shortcut.
steps.see: The Run tool window opens and asks for your name; type it there and press Enter.

steps.do: Change the greeting, then rerun the last run configuration.
Open Run | Edit Configurations to see the configuration PyCharm made for greet.py: its script path, parameters and interpreter.

lab.title: Set up your Python workspace
lab.goal: Create a PyCharm project with its own virtual environment, install a package into it, and run a script that proves everything is wired up.
setup: PyCharm installed (the free version is enough)
Python 3 installed from python.org or your system's package manager

steps.do: Create a new Pure Python project called hello-pycharm with a new virtual environment (venv) inside it.
Install the requests package into the project's environment from the Python Packages tool window, or in PyCharm's Terminal.
Create a file called check_setup.py with this code. Let completion type the long names for you.
steps.code:
import sys

import requests

print("Python", sys.version.split()[0])
print("Running from", sys.prefix)
print("requests", requests.__version__)

steps.do: Run check_setup.py.
steps.see: Three lines: the Python version, the environment's folder (ending in .venv or venv) and the version of requests.

steps.do: Break it on purpose: change requests to requestz in the import. PyCharm underlines it in red; hover over it to read why. Change it back.
Make a requirements file in the Terminal so others could recreate the environment.

checks.text: It runs from the project's own virtual environment, not the system's Python.
The requests package is installed in that environment and its version is printed.

lab.submit: Paste the three lines check_setup.py printed in the Run tool window.
hints: If the output shows a folder without venv in it, the project is using the system interpreter: choose the virtual environment in Settings | Project | Python Interpreter.

modules.title: Python essentials in the editor
modules.summary: Values and types, decisions and loops, and Python's collections, with an editor that completes your code and fixes mistakes as you type.

lessons.title: Values, variables and types
objectives: Use Python's basic types and convert between them
Let PyCharm's completion, documentation and quick-fixes help you write code
key_points: Python's basic types include int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text), bool (True or False) and None, which means no value.
Python is dynamically typed: a variable can refer to a value of any type, and type(x) tells you which type it holds now.
Converting changes a value's type: int('42') is the number 42 and str(42) is the text '42'; int('forty') raises a ValueError.
An f-string such as f'{name} is {age}' puts values into text; f'{price:.2f}' shows a number with two decimal places.
PyCharm checks your code as you type: errors are underlined in red, and Show Context Actions offers fixes, such as adding a missing import.

steps.do: In a new file, type price = 4 and then pri. Open basic completion if it hasn't appeared.
Type round( and see what arguments it takes.
steps.see: A hint showing round(number, ndigits=None).

steps.do: Put the caret on round and read its documentation without leaving the editor.
Type math.sqrt(16) without importing math. It's underlined in red. Put the caret on it and open Show Context Actions, then choose Import 'math'.
steps.see: import math is added at the top of the file.

steps.do: Print the type of a few values to check what you think they are.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops: if, for and while
objectives: Write if, elif and else to choose between actions
Repeat work with for and while loops
key_points: Python marks blocks of code by indentation, usually four spaces: the lines indented under an if or a for belong to it.
if, elif and else run the first block whose condition is true; comparisons such as ==, !=, < and >= give True or False.
A for loop runs once for each item in a sequence; range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true, so something in the loop must eventually make it false.
break leaves a loop straight away, and continue skips to the loop's next round.

steps.do: Write a loop that counts down, but leave the indentation messy on purpose.
Reformat the file to tidy spacing and indentation.
Select two print lines and wrap them in an if or a for with Surround With.
Insert a live template: open the list and choose one, such as main for an if __name__ == '__main__': block.
Comment out a line, and back in, with one shortcut.

lessons.title: Lists, dictionaries and other collections
objectives: Choose between lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets
Explore data interactively in the Python Console
key_points: A list holds items in order and can change: scores = [88, 92, 79]; scores.append(100) adds one, and scores[0] is the first.
A tuple is like a list that can't be changed after it's made, which suits fixed groups of values such as a point (3, 4).
A dictionary maps keys to values, as in ages = {'Amara': 31}; ages['Amara'] looks a value up and raises KeyError if the key is missing.
A set holds unique items with no order, which makes it quick to remove duplicates or test membership.
A list comprehension builds a list in one line: [s * 2 for s in scores if s > 80].

walkthrough.title: Explore data in the Python Console

steps.do: Open Tools | Python or Debug Console. It runs in your project's interpreter.
steps.see: A console with a variables pane beside it.

steps.do: Type a dictionary and a list into the console, one at a time, and watch them appear in the variables pane, where you can expand them.
In the editor, write a few lines that use them, select the lines and send them to the console with Execute Selection in Python Console.
steps.code:
doubled = [s * 2 for s in scores if s > 80]
print(doubled)

steps.do: Look up a key that isn't there, ages['Lena'], and read the KeyError. Then try ages.get('Lena', 0), which returns a default instead.

lab.title: Build a grade book
lab.goal: Finish a grade book program that works out each student's average and letter grade, then the class average.
setup: Your hello-pycharm project, or a new one
Download the starter file grades.py and put it in the project

steps.do: Open grades.py. The TODO comments say what each function must do. Open the TODO tool window (View | Tool Windows | TODO) to see them all in one list.
Write average(scores): the sum of the scores divided by how many there are, rounded to 1 decimal place with round(value, 1).
Write letter(avg) with if, elif and else: A from 90, B from 80, C from 70, D from 60, otherwise F.
Write main(): loop over SCORES.items(), print each student's line with an f-string, keep their averages in a list, and print the mean of that list rounded to 1 decimal place.
Run grades.py and compare your output with the expected lines below.
steps.see: Amara: 86.3 (B), Kofi: 64.3 (D), Lena: 97.7 (A), Ravi: 77.0 (C), then Class average: 81.3

Each student gets the right letter grade.
The class average is printed and right.

modules.title: Functions, modules and files
modules.summary: Organise code into functions and modules, read and write files, and handle errors, with refactoring and navigation that keep a growing project tidy.

lessons.title: Writing functions
objectives: Define functions with parameters, defaults and return values
Extract and rename functions safely with PyCharm
key_points: A function is a named, reusable block of code defined with def; it takes inputs called parameters and can give back a result with return.
A function without a return statement returns None.
Parameters can have default values, as in def greet(name, greeting='Hello'), and callers can pass arguments by name: greet('Amara', greeting='Hi').
A docstring, a string on the first line of a function, says what it does; type hints such as def area(r: float) -> float: document what it expects.
Small functions that each do one thing are easier to test, reuse and understand than one long script.

walkthrough.title: Extract a function, then rename it everywhere

steps.do: Select a few lines that work something out, for example the lines that compute an average.
steps.see: Each press of Extend Selection selects a bigger piece of code.

steps.do: Turn them into a function with Extract Method and give it a name.
steps.see: A new function, with the selected lines replaced by a call to it.

steps.do: Rename the function: PyCharm updates every call to it, in every file.
Find everywhere the function is used.
From a call, jump to the function's definition, and back again.

lessons.title: Modules, packages and imports
objectives: Split a program into modules and import from them
Navigate a project quickly with the keyboard
key_points: Every .py file is a module; import tracker loads it, and from tracker import load_expenses brings in one name.
A package is a folder of modules; Python's standard library includes many, such as csv, json, math, pathlib and datetime.
Code under if __name__ == '__main__': runs only when the file is run directly, not when another module imports it.
Imports go at the top of a file: standard library first, then installed packages, then your own modules.

walkthrough.title: Find your way around a project

steps.do: Open any file in the project by typing part of its name in Go to File.
Jump to a function or class anywhere in the project with Go to Symbol.
Switch between the files you opened most recently.
See the outline of the current file, its functions and classes, in a popup.
Remove unused imports and sort the rest.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files, and handling errors
objectives: Read and write text and CSV files safely
Handle errors with try and except instead of crashing
key_points: open(path, encoding='utf-8') opens a file; using it in a with block closes the file for you, even if something goes wrong.
The csv module reads spreadsheet-like files: csv.DictReader gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header row's names.
When something goes wrong Python raises an exception, such as FileNotFoundError or ValueError; try and except catch one so you can handle it.
Catch only the exceptions you expect and can do something about; a bare except hides bugs you'd want to see.

steps.do: Open the Problems tool window to see every error and warning in the file.
Jump to the next highlighted problem in the editor.
Read the full description of a problem under the caret.
Write a with block that reads a CSV file. Type wi and accept the completion, then let PyCharm suggest csv.DictReader once csv is imported.
steps.code:
import csv

with open("expenses.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["category"], row["amount"])

modules.title: Debugging like a professional
modules.summary: Stop guessing: pause programs with breakpoints, step through them line by line, inspect their state and read tracebacks to the line that went wrong.

lessons.title: Breakpoints and stepping through code
objectives: Pause a program at a breakpoint and step through it
Read variables and the call stack while it's paused
key_points: A debugger runs your program under your control: it pauses at breakpoints so you can see exactly what the code is doing.
Step Over runs the current line and stops at the next one; Step Into goes inside a function the line calls; Step Out finishes the current function.
While a program is paused, the Variables pane shows the value of every variable in scope.
The Frames list (the call stack) shows which function called which to reach the current line.

steps.do: Click in the gutter beside a line, or put the caret on it and toggle a line breakpoint.
steps.see: A red dot beside the line.

steps.do: Start debugging: click the green arrow in the gutter beside if __name__ == '__main__': and choose Debug, or debug the last run configuration.
steps.see: The program stops at the breakpoint and the Debug tool window opens.

steps.do: Step over the current line.
Step into the function this line calls.
Step out of the function, back to its caller.
Resume the program until the next breakpoint, or the end.

lessons.title: Inspecting state: expressions, watches and conditions
objectives: Evaluate expressions while a program is paused
Use conditional breakpoints to stop only when something interesting happens
key_points: Evaluate Expression runs any Python expression in the paused program, such as len(cart) or total * 0.9, to test an idea without editing the code.
A watch keeps an expression in view and updates it after every step.
A conditional breakpoint pauses only when its condition is true, such as i == 99 in a long loop.
Run to Cursor runs until the line the caret is on, without a permanent breakpoint.

steps.do: While paused, open Evaluate Expression, type an expression and press Enter.
Add a watch: in the Debug tool window's Variables pane, use the + button (New Watch) and type an expression, such as total.
Right-click a breakpoint's red dot and type a condition, so it only stops when it's true.
See and manage all your breakpoints in one place.
Put the caret on a later line and run to it.

lessons.title: Reading tracebacks and fixing common bugs
objectives: Read a traceback to find where and why a program failed
Recognise Python's most common bugs
key_points: A traceback lists the calls that led to an error, the most recent last; its final line names the exception and its message.
In PyCharm's Run tool window, the file and line in a traceback are links that open the line that failed.
Common errors include NameError (a name that doesn't exist), TypeError (a value of the wrong type), IndexError (a position past the end of a list) and KeyError (a missing dictionary key).
Off-by-one errors, such as a range that starts at 1 instead of 0, skip or repeat an item without raising any error at all.
A default argument such as cart=[] is created once and shared by every call; use cart=None and make a new list inside the function.

steps.do: Run a script that crashes and find the last line of the traceback: the exception and what it says.
steps.see: IndexError: list index out of range

steps.do: Click the link to the file and line in the traceback to jump straight to it.
Put a breakpoint on that line and debug the program to see the values that led to the crash.
Fix the line, then rerun to confirm.

lab.title: Fix the buggy shopping cart
lab.goal: Use the debugger to find and fix three bugs in a small shopping cart program. Each bug gives a wrong answer without crashing, which is why guessing doesn't work.
setup: Download the starter file cart.py into a PyCharm project

steps.do: Run cart.py and write down what it prints. With notebooks (2 x 4.50), pens (5 x 1.20) and a backpack (35.00), the morning cart should have 3 items and cost 45.00 after 10% off, and the evening cart should have 1 item.
steps.see: Morning cart: 4 item(s), total after 10% off: 49.90, and Evening cart: 4 item(s). Both wrong.

steps.do: Put a breakpoint on the first line of main() and debug it.
Step over each add_item call and watch morning and evening in the Variables pane. Why does the evening cart already hold the morning's items?
Step into subtotal() and watch i and total change with each round of the loop. Which item is never added?
While paused in apply_discount(), use Evaluate Expression to try amount - percent / 100 and amount * (1 - percent / 100).
Fix all three bugs and run cart.py again.
steps.see: Morning cart: 3 item(s), total after 10% off: 45.00, and Evening cart: 1 item(s)

checks.text: The morning cart has 3 items and costs 45.00 after the discount.
The evening cart has only its own item.
The shared default list is fixed: add_item uses cart=None and makes a new list when none is given.
Each bug is explained in a sentence, including how the debugger showed it.

lab.submit: Paste your fixed cart.py, its output, and a sentence for each bug: what was wrong and how the debugger helped you find it.

files.content:
"""A shopping cart with three bugs in it. Find them with PyCharm's debugger, not by guessing."""


def add_item(name, price, quantity=1, cart=[]):
    cart.append({"name": name, "price": price, "quantity": quantity})
    return cart


def subtotal(cart):
    total = 0
    for i in range(1, len(cart)):
        total += cart[i]["price"] * cart[i]["quantity"]
    return total


def apply_discount(amount, percent):
    """Take percent off amount: 10 percent off 50.00 is 45.00."""
    return amount - percent / 100


def main():
    morning = add_item("notebook", 4.50, 2)
    add_item("pen", 1.20, 5, morning)
    add_item("backpack", 35.00, 1, morning)

    evening = add_item("water bottle", 9.00)

    total = apply_discount(subtotal(morning), 10)
    print(f"Morning cart: {len(morning)} item(s), total after 10% off: {total:.2f}")
    print(f"Evening cart: {len(evening)} item(s)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: range(1, len(cart)) starts at the second item.
10 percent off is amount * 0.9, not amount - 0.1.

modules.title: Testing, refactoring and Git
modules.summary: Make code you can trust and change: unit tests with pytest, refactoring with tests to protect you, and version control with Git, all from inside PyCharm.

lessons.title: Unit tests with pytest
objectives: Write unit tests with pytest
Run tests and read their results in PyCharm
key_points: A unit test is a small piece of code that checks one piece of your code gives the result you expect.
pytest finds tests by name: files called test_*.py or *_test.py, and functions in them whose names start with test.
A test uses assert to state what must be true, such as assert total_by_category([]) == {}; when an assert fails, pytest shows the values on each side.
Running tests after every change tells you at once if the change broke something that used to work.

walkthrough.title: Write and run tests in PyCharm

steps.do: Install pytest into the project's environment from the Python Packages tool window, or in the Terminal.
In Settings, go to Tools | Python Integrated Tools and set Default test runner to pytest.
Create a file named test_tracker.py next to tracker.py and write a test function in it.
Run the test with the green arrow beside it in the gutter, or run the test under the caret.
steps.see: The Run tool window shows a test tree with a green tick and 1 passed.

steps.do: Break the test on purpose (expect {'food': 1}) and run it again. Click the failed test to see the difference between the expected and the actual value, then put it right and use Rerun Failed Tests.
Jump between tracker.py and its test with Go to Test.

lessons.title: Refactoring safely
objectives: Explain what refactoring is and why tests make it safe
Use PyCharm's automated refactorings
key_points: Refactoring changes how code is structured without changing what it does, to make it easier to read and change.
Tests make refactoring safe: run them before and after, and if they still pass, the behaviour hasn't changed.
Automated refactorings, such as rename, extract and inline, update every place the code is used, which hand edits can miss.
Refactor in small steps, running the tests after each one, so any mistake is easy to find.

steps.do: Run your tests first, so you know they pass before you change anything.
Open the list of refactorings available where the caret is.
Give a long expression a name with Extract Variable.
Do the opposite with Inline, when a variable's name adds nothing.
Add a parameter to a function, or reorder them, with Change Signature: every call is updated.
If a change goes wrong, right-click the file and choose Local History | Show History to see and restore earlier versions, even without Git.

lessons.title: Version control with Git in PyCharm
objectives: Explain what Git records and why developers use it
Commit, view history and push from PyCharm
key_points: Git is a version control system: it records snapshots of your project, called commits, so you can see what changed, when and why, and go back.
Each commit has a message that explains the change; small commits with clear messages make history useful.
A .gitignore file lists what Git should leave out, such as the virtual environment folder (.venv) and caches.
A branch is a separate line of work, so you can try something without disturbing the main version.
Pushing sends your commits to a remote repository, such as one on GitHub, where others can see them and they're backed up.

walkthrough.title: Your first commits from the IDE

steps.do: Put the project under Git: VCS | Create Git Repository (or VCS | Enable Version Control Integration, then choose Git).
Add a .gitignore file at the project's top level that leaves out the virtual environment and caches.
Open the Commit tool window, tick the files to include, write a message such as Add expense tracker, and commit.
Open the Git tool window and its Log tab to see your history.
Create a branch from the branch name in the toolbar (New Branch), make a change there and commit it.
When you have a GitHub repository to push to, push your commits.

Put the project under Git, add a .gitignore that leaves out .venv/ and __pycache__/, and commit with the message Add tests for the tracker.
In PyCharm's Terminal, run the tests once more and show your history.

checks.text: There's a test for an empty list of expenses.
The work is committed to Git with a clear message.

lab.submit: Paste test_tracker.py, the summary line pytest printed, and the output of git log --oneline.
hints: If pytest can't import tracker, make sure test_tracker.py is in the same folder as tracker.py and that you run it from the project's top level.

project.title: Build a study tracker
project.brief: Build a command-line study tracker in PyCharm. It lets you record study sessions (a date, a subject and how many minutes), saves them to a file so they're still there next time, and reports your total minutes per subject and your longest streak of days in a row. Structure it as functions in more than one module, handle bad input and a missing data file without crashing, test it with pytest, and keep its history in Git with small, clear commits.
deliverables: The source code: at least two modules, with functions that each do one thing
A test file with at least five pytest tests, all passing
A README.md that explains how to run the program and the tests
The output of a run that adds sessions and prints the report
The output of git log --oneline, showing at least four commits

rubric.name: It works
rubric.description: Sessions can be added and are saved between runs; the report's totals per subject and the streak are right.

rubric.name: Code structure and readability
rubric.description: Code is split into well-named functions and modules, with docstrings, consistent formatting and no repeated blocks.

rubric.name: Handling problems
rubric.description: Bad input (such as minutes that aren't a number) and a missing or empty data file give clear messages, not tracebacks.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: At least five meaningful pytest tests that cover normal cases and edge cases, such as no sessions or a single day, and all pass.

rubric.name: IDE and Git workflow
rubric.description: A README explains how to run it; the Git history has small commits with clear messages and a .gitignore that leaves out the virtual environment.

project.submit: Paste your code (each module, with its file name), your tests, your README, the output of a run, the pytest summary and your git log --oneline. A link to a public repository is welcome too.
